The UNSC resolution to begin the process of removing Saddam from office was passed on December 10, 2003. It was the first of a series of resolutions designed to eliminate Saddam's regime in a way that would minimize the chances that Iraq would ever attack the United Nations or the UNAMI. After Saddam was removed, the Security Council decided to create a special tribunal for the trials of Iraq's former leaders. That tribunal, known as the Special Tribunal for Iraq (STPI), was designed not only to try Saddam, but also to prosecute the former Iraqi leaders and their supporters for war crimes and other crimes against humanity. In July 2006, a court in The Hague acquitted all seven former members of Saddam Husseins regime, ruling that they were not responsible for crimes committed against the Iraqis during the Gulf War. But the court also ruled that Saddam had ordered the killings of tens of thousands of Iraqi civilians in order to weaken his enemies. This ruling was appealed, with the appeal being heard in 2008. Ultimately, in September 2009 the Court of Appeals of The Netherlands dismissed the case of the seven defendants, saying that there was no evidence that any of them were responsible. They were however convicted for violating the laws of war. Saddam Hussain was convicted of crimes of genocide, war criminals, crimes in connection with war, torture and crimes relating to the death of at least 100,000 Iraqi civilian in his regime. On December 21, 2011, Saddam died in hospital in Baghdad from complications of an infection. He had been suffering from diabetes since 2005 and was suffering with severe kidney failure. Hair color varies among individuals of the same species. Certain animals, such as dogs, have a light or reddish coloration, whereas others, like humans, are generally darker in their hair.
Hair color is an important consideration in many species, because it provides camouflage and protection from predators. In addition, hair may serve as a signal in certain situations. For example, if hair is lost in a predator's attack, it may indicate that the prey animal is dead. However, this is only an indication of a temporary loss of pigment, not a loss that is permanent. Therefore, a hair loss, even in humans and other mammals, does not necessarily mean that a person is dying. A person's hair does tend to thin out over time, but this does depend on factors such a the person and their lifestyle. Some people, for example those with albinism, will have their hairs completely lose their pigmentation (loss of color) at some point in life. A national party may also have state affiliates, or may have a national organization that works with state parties and state-level organizations to coordinate campaigns and organize votes. CHAPTER 1 The Beginning of Physics 1 THE MATTER OF THE SPIN A few words about the spin of an electron are sufficient to introduce the notion of spin in the modern world, even if this concept is not generally used in physics textbooks. Spin is an intrinsic property of electrons, or any other particle, that is described by an axis that runs through the particle. For example, if an atom of iron is placed on a table and a magnet is put above it, then the electrons in it will be oriented in a particular direction. The mandolo is a cross between a guitar and a mandolina, although it has a different construction, as well as a lower neck. This is because of its use as the accompaniment to the Celtic flute and the guitar. A modern mandolone is usually made of metal, but the ancient mandolar was made from a variety of woods and materials. These include: the Spanish guitar (a cross-section of a classical guitar with a curved neck), the Italian guitar or mandorla (like a lute), and other types of guitars. Some mandolas are made in various sizes (for example, a small mando is small enough for a child to play while a large one is suitable for adults), whereas others are single or double strings. However, all mandolis are used to accompany the flutes. Today, mandoles are often used as solo instruments, especially in flamenco, rock, jazz, classical, or folk music; they can also be used with other instruments such as trumpets, flugelhorns, cellos, violin, viola, trombones, guitars, drums and percussion instruments (including cymbals), or the like. Locke's views were to some extent in reaction to Descartes's (1596–1650) ideas about the soul and the human mind as a machine, but in the end he was to draw on Descartists' understanding of the universe (and his own) in his idea of self-consciousness. This led him to believe that human beings have a rational soul which is separate from the physical body. From Locke, then, we have the idea that reason is something that can be known through experience, and we can then extend this to include the other senses. While Locke thought that only the body is real, the rational mind is an idea with a reality that transcends the bounds of materialism. Thus, while Locke did not conceive of reason as knowledge, he did conceive it as something to which human reason could give access. In other words, human knowledge could be conceived of as having a basis in reason. According to Locke this basis is, by definition, not a material thing, since it can only be understood through human experience and can therefore not be seen to have any properties or properties that are independent of human perception or experience (see also Locke’s philosophy of nature). In the case of HIV infection, for example, the identification and classification of patients infected with HIV is based on the fact that the virus has a unique genetic code, which is referred to as the HIV genome. A variety of methods exist for the determination of this unique DNA sequence. The most widely used method is the polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
The PCR is a method of amplifying a target nucleic acid sequence by the use of DNA polymerase and the target sequence as a template. In this method, a set of primers is used to amplify a region of a nucleic molecule that is complementary to a portion of that molecule. Once the region is amplified, it can be analyzed by any of several techniques, including gel electrophoresis. This technique allows the detection of unique sequences for each patient, and can determine whether the patient has been infected by a particular agent. Thus, PCR technology is commonly used in diagnostic laboratories to identify a disease caused by an agent, such as HIV. However, there is no assay for detecting HIV in blood. There are, however, several commercial kits for detection and quantification of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) in serum. These kits usually involve a centrifugation procedure, in which the serum is separated from the blood cells and then tested for HIV antibodies by testing for viral antigens. Although the sensitivity of these assays is good, they are not sufficiently sensitive for use in a clinical laboratory setting. Therefore, even though these kits are useful in detecting the presence of antibodies, none of them is sufficiently accurate to be clinically useful.

Nisbett in his book (New York, Harcourt Brace, 1963). N. B. is known to be a strong advocate of collective action theory (CAS) and he is credited with popularizing the concept. According to CAS, the behavior of individuals is influenced by their perceptions of social groups. The term "social perception" is used to refer to an individual's beliefs about the nature and function of other individuals in the same or different social group as that of which he or she is part.Nisbet explains that social perception is an amalgamation of three factors. First, a subject's perceptions are influenced in part by his or her degree of identification with the groups involved. Second, social perceptions also are affected by factors that are related to what the subject believes to exist in groups such as the norms and values of that group, or the status of individual members in that same group; third, and perhaps most importantly, all of these factors are also influenced, sometimes in varying degrees, by external influences such factors as social events, media messages, political ideologies, etc.
The individual in whom the perception of being part of another group is stronger is also more likely to have a stronger and more persistent social impression. On the basis of this social influence, individuals can then adopt a more or less inclusive (or exclusive) boundary with respect to other groups and individuals. Animals with high metabolic rates, including humans, have a wide range of body temperatures, with some of them reaching higher than 40°C (104°F).The body's core temperature, or core body temp, is the temperature of its core, usually the muscle or bone marrow, where the animal's metabolic rate is high. Core body temps are influenced by a number of factors, ranging from the type of food ingested to the activity level of an individual. They are also influenced through the action of hormones, in particular the thyroid. Although most animals have well-marked thermoneutral zones, there is some variation between individuals. Many mammals have more than one thermoregulatory zone. In some, the thermal preference for one zone predominates, whereas in others it is more balanced. As a result, an animal can have one or more zones of higher or lower temperature depending on its metabolic activity. These variations in thermotaxis are likely to affect the efficiency of heat exchange and thus the rate of metabolism. Because of this, it has been suggested that animals with more efficient thermoreception could have evolved more quickly, increasing the chances of their survival. A higher thermal tolerance can also be advantageous to an organism in some circumstances, as in cold environments, because it allows more time for metabolic processes to take place before the body is chilled. When mammals are exposed to high ambient temperatures they may use their fur to insulate them from heat loss, allowing them to maintain body heat.

In response to the new FCC proposal, net-neutrality opponents, including the Electronic Frontier Foundation and the Center for Democracy and Technology, have called for a global protest against the FCC's proposal. On 13 April, Net Neutrality Alliance (NNA) president David Boies wrote a letter to FCC Chairman Tom Wheeler, and other members of the commission, expressing opposition to reclassification. Boie writes, "Reclassification would undermine the promise of net Neutrals to consumers, innovators and competition by allowing the incumbents to create a 'fast lane' to their favored content and services."
Boies argues that re-classification is unnecessary because net providers already offer fast lanes to other content players, such as Netflix, Pandora, Amazon, Spotify, Hulu, YouTube, Apple, Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile and Sprint. He also argues reining in fast lane content is not in the public interest, arguing that "there is no evidence that fast-lane services are more efficient, more reliable, or more affordable than traditional services, nor is there any evidence of significant harm to competition." Boys also writes that the Internet is already a fast network, not a slow one, because there are a variety of ways to access content on the net, like streaming and downloading. Boiese further argues the reclassified broadband would be a "waste of money", because the money could be spent on broadband and internet access, rather than new, faster networks. Finally, Boise argues "the FCC is attempting to overturn the will of Congress and replace the neutrality of Net neutrality with a biased and inefficient scheme."

text: In the United States, for example, there were two different kinds of technical institute: technical colleges (which became technical universities) and polytechnical institiutes. Technical colleges were state-supported, while polytech institudes were privately financed. The differences between these instituions were often related to the number, type of degree programs offered and the location of their campuses. Polytechnic institues were generally located in smaller cities, and in the Midwest. A typical poly tech institute included a department of engineering, a college of business, an agriculture program, or a humanities program. Most poly technics also had an industrial program and an agricultural program or two. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, many poly technical institutions were closed due to budgetary constraints. However, in many cases, they were revived in later decades. Some of these poly technological instituiates were later converted into universities, such as the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Others were converted to other types of colleges, including technical schools, which are now in general use in America. Many poly techno institucies still exist today in some countries and are still considered poly technology institutues. They are usually located within larger universities. For example: the Polytech Institute of the Philippines is a technical university; the Technical College of India is located near the Bangalore, India, campus of IIM-Bangalore; and, the College de Polytecnics of Japan is an institute of polytechnology located close to Tokyo, Japan. Different phases of digestion take place including: the cephalic phase, gastric phase, and intestinal phase.The cephalic phase occurs at the sight, thought and smell of food, which stimulate the cerebral cortex. This phase is followed by the gastric part of the digestive tract, the duodenum, jejunum, ileum and colon, where the food is broken down into its component parts and the nutrients absorbed. The intestinal part, known as the caecum, then digests the rest.During the intestinal digestion, enzymes digest the complex carbohydrates and other nutrients in the diet. It is this portion of digestive digestion that is most affected by diet, not the cecumber, because it is the last phase in digestion and cannot be influenced by a change in diet.
During this stage, food passes through the pylorus. As the stomach empties, it forms a barrier to prevent food from reaching the small intestine.
The first part to be digested is a sugar solution called a chyme, or thick, liquid. During this phase the pancreas secretes a large amount of enzymes, including amylases and lipases. These enzymes work to break down and digest a broad range of carbohydrates in chylomicrons, small intestinal cells. In the second part the chymicalyte is emptied into the intestines. Here the enzymes are working to make the sugars available to the bacteria in order to use it as energy for growth. At the third part in this process, a carbohydrate is absorbed into cells of a tissue, for example, fat cells and glycogen. Finally, at this part is when enzymes break the fats down to a simpler form, such as fatty acids. All of this happens within the first three hours of an individual’s digestion. Some foodstuffs are better than others at breaking down, with some being more difficult to digest than other. They include some fruits and vegetables such a apples, bananas, pears, onions, etc. Other foods, like bread, rice, pasta, potatoes, cereals and certain meat and fish, are easier to process than these. Foods that are not easily digested by humans include fat, salt, alcohol, sugar, spices, coffee, tea and most animal products.
